1. Approach and rationale

1.1 Central idea

The task is a finite-dimensional nonlinear minimax problem.  The planner constructs a discrete function h represented by a one-dimensional NumPy vector of length n and seeks to minimize

    C(h) = dx * max_r np.correlate(h, 1-h, mode="full")[r],   dx = 2/n,

subject to

    0 <= h_i <= 1,   sum_i h_i = n/2.

The proposed algorithm is based on two exact structural observations and one local optimization discipline.

First, the full finite-support objective includes all lag signs.  Invariance under the transformation

    T(h)_i = 1 - h_{n-1-i}

is immediate at the level of the complete lag set: a term corresponding to one lag is transformed into the reversed term corresponding to the opposite lag.  Therefore evaluating h or T(h) with np.correlate over all full lags gives the same maximum.

Second, the constraint sum(h)=n/2 can be made exact automatically if we restrict to the symmetric-complement subspace

    h_i = a_i,     h_{n-1-i} = 1 - a_i

with 0 <= a_i <= 1.  For odd n, the centre entry is fixed to 0.5.  Any value of the reduced vector a in [0,1] produces a perfectly feasible full vector, in real arithmetic, without clipping followed by sum rescaling.  This eliminates the equality constraint entirely and reduces the decision dimension from n to ceil(n/2), with only simple box bounds remaining.

Third, the main promotion mechanism is exact-score local descent.  The optimizer is not driven only by a smooth surrogate or by an unviewed linearized objective.  At each current symmetric vector a, the algorithm:

1. computes the exact original objective for candidate moves;
2. identifies active finite-support correlation constraints using exact correlation rows and gradients;
3. forms candidate directions by an active-constraint linearized least-squares model, negative active gradients, and several deterministic transformations;
4. performs an exact one-dimensional search along each direction in the symmetric box and accepts only exact improvements;
5. refines promising candidates with a direct minimax nonlinear program formulated only in reduced symmetric variables, using SLSQP and exact row gradients.

The algorithm explores this reduced symmetric family from many starting points: the supplied parent, symmetrized/interpolated parents, binary complement patterns, cosine and logistic patterns, random symmetric patterns, and offspring combinations.  All candidates are scored by the original evaluator.  The main limitation is that the problem remains bilinear and nonconvex, and symmetric reduction is not claimed to contain the global optimum.  Nevertheless it gives a strong local optimizer with exact feasibility, reduced coordinates, and a direct model for the largest constraints.

1.2 Why this addresses the computational bottleneck

The supplied parent is already near record quality.  Small improvements normally violate some nonactive lag constraints when attempting only a single descent direction.  The active-correlation tangent model is aimed at this bottleneck: several large constraints are linearized and exploited simultaneously through a least-squares direction.  Candidate moves are then checked exactly, so an inactive constraint cannot be accepted if it becomes larger.

The symmetric parameterization is the second key improvement.  Ordinary optimization must either add an equality constraint or use a joint projection after every update.  Here the equality is imposed automatically by the design.  The optimizer has half as many variables, no equality row Jacobian, and no post-update sum repair.  This improves numerical conditioning and makes closed-form gradients easy to verify.

1.3 Honest limitations and hypotheses

The exact local formulation uses bilinear objectives and is not convex.  A constrained local solve is accepted only if the original np.correlate score improves.  SLSQP should be regarded as a local polish, not a certificate of global optimality.  Symmetric-complement search is a heuristic restriction intended to contain excellent records, based on invariance and the observed use of complement-reflection in this class of problems; it is not invoked as a proven missing minimizer.  The raw supplied parent remains a valid fallback whenever it is feasible.  If the search remains nonempty, the program always returns a discrete feasible vector and a bound recomputed from that vector.

2. Mathematical specification

2.1 Discrete representation and exact score

For an integer n>=1, define dx=2/n and target sum s=n/2.  For any full vector h of length n, the official score is exactly

    S(h) = dx * max_r np.correlate(h, 1.0-h, mode="full")[r].

The accepted objective must be computed by this formula (or an evaluator supplied by the harness after verifying completion).  All decisions, candidate acceptance, best storage, and the return bound must use this expression.

Feasibility is first checked in final full coordinates:

    finite: all entries finite;
    box: -eps_box <= h_i <= 1 + eps_box;
    sum: |sum(h) - n/2| <= eps_sum.

Choose a small numerical tolerance, e.g.

    eps_box = 1e-11,
    eps_sum = 1e-10 * max(1, n).

An unenforced candidate with larger violation must be corrected by the joint feasibility helper described below or discarded.

2.2 Manual full-lag correlation and gradient rows

For directed gradients and active-set constructions, implement a manual row for every integer lag k separated by the evaluator sister to the “full” collection.  This does not replace acceptance; it must match it after permutation.

For n and k = -(n-1), -(n-2), ..., n-1, valid i satisfy

    0 <= i < n,
    0 <= i+k < n,

or equivalently

    start(k) = max(0,-k),
    end(k)   = min(n,n-k),

where end(k) is Python-exclusive.  The unscaled correlation row is

    F_k(h) = sum_{i=start(k)}^{end(k)-1} h_i * (1 - h_{i+k}).

The scaled objective row is

    C_k(h) = dx * F_k(h).

For each row define its unscaled gradient G_k in R^n.  Each pair (i,j=i+k) in the support contributes to F_k:

    h_i - h_i*h_j.

Consequently:

    at index i: add 1 - h_j;
    at index j: add -h_i.

Use accumulation over each coordinate.  The diagonal k=0 case is covered correctly by the rules:

    derivative for h_p(1-h_p) = (1-h_p) + (-h_p) = 1 - 2*h_p.

Return a matrix of gradients parallel to the value rows.  The row order does not need to match np.correlate’s output order, but the set of scaled values must be a permutation of np.correlate output for a defensive consistency check before derivative-dependent optimization.  If this check fails, skip derivative-dependent phases and fall back to the non-derivative or parent fallback mechanisms.

2.3 Symmetric-complement parameterization

Let

    m = floor(n/2).

For any u in R^m with 0 <= u_j <= 1, define a full vector H(u) by

    for j=0,...,m-1:
        H(u)_j = u_j,
        H(u)_{n-1-j} = 1 - u_j.

If n is odd, define the middle entry

    H(u)_{m} = 0.5.

Then:

    sum_j H(u)_j + possibly 0.5 = m + 0.5 = n/2.

The box follows entrywise from 0 <= u <= 1 and 1-u in [0,1].  The pair identity holds in exact real arithmetic; floating-point pair cancellation should normally satisfy eps_sum, with a final fine correction in Section 3.11.

A full vector h can be projected into this subspace by the linear symmetrization

    H_sym = 0.5 * (h + 1 - h_reverse).

If h <= 1 in real arithmetic (or after clipping in the machine implementation), H_sym also lies in [0,1].  The projection enforces the sum exactly:

    sum(H_sym) = 0.5*sum(h) + 0.5*n - 0.5*sum(h) = n/2.

A variable vector extracted from full H_sym is

    u = (H_sym[0], H_sym[1], ..., H_sym[m-1]).

When recovering u from a general full vector, first symmetrize.  Direct treatment of non-symmetric full vectors using this representation is not used; instead the exact H_sym copy is constructed first.

2.4 Reduction of correlation derivatives to u variables

Because H(u) has only pair-varying entries, full-row gradients normalize to row gradients on u.  For a full-row gradient g of shape (n,), the reduced row is

    for j=0,...,m-1:
        g_U_j = g_j - g_{n-1-j}.

The centre coordinate for odd n has coefficient zero and is not included.

For each correlation row F_k, if G_k is its full unscaled gradient, the reduced-row gradient is

    A_k^U[j] = G_k[j] - G_k[n-1-j].

The official reduced correlation value can be obtained equivalently as S(U) = S(H(U)).  A defensive check can compare the maximum of dx times reduced correlation values generated by the manual row set against S(H(U)); at the level of maximum, agreement is required.  The actual full evaluator used for objective comparison should be applied to H(U).

2.5 Direct reduced minimax formulation

The reduced variable vector has length m+1:

    z = (u_0, ..., u_{m-1}, theta).

Bounds:

    0 <= u_j <= 1,
    0 <= theta <= 1.5 (theta cannot influence the final exact candidate, but a near-bounded range prevents numerical drifting).

Objective and gradient:

    f(z) = theta,
    ∂f/∂u_j = 0,
    ∂f/∂theta = 1.

Constraint for each manual row k:

    c_k(z) = theta - dx * F_k(H(U(z))) >= 0,

with row inputs A^U_k the reduced gradients defined above.  Its Jacobian is:

    ∂c_k/∂u_j = -dx * A^U_k[j],
    ∂c_k/∂theta = 1.

The inequality rows must cover all lags or non-redundant signed-positive lags.  For implementation simplicity and a row-match future safety, use the full 2n-1 rows.
